subject: maths
title: Primary 4 Angles: Naming, Measuring and Drawing Angles
seo_title: P4 Angles Worksheets: Free Primary 4 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: Using notation such as ∠ABC and ∠a to name angles; measuring angles in degrees; drawing an angle of given size
meta_desc: Free P4 maths practice on angles: name ∠ABC, acute or obtuse, read a protractor, turns and clocks. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: In ∠ABC the vertex B is the middle letter, and you read the protractor scale that starts at 0.
key_sub: An acute angle that reads 50 on one scale and 130 on the other is 50°.
body_html:
Naming angles

An angle is made by two arms that meet at a point, the vertex. We name an angle with three letters, and the vertex is always the middle letter. We can also name an angle with one small letter, like ∠a.

Acute, right and obtuse

We measure angles in degrees (°). Compare an angle with a right angle (90°).

The length of the arms does not change the size of an angle. Only the amount of turn matters.

Measure with a protractor

1. Put the centre of the protractor on the vertex. 2. Line up one arm with 0. 3. Read the scale that starts at 0 on that arm. 4. Check with your estimate: acute or obtuse?

Draw ∠PQR = 65°

Draw the line QR. Put the centre of the protractor on Q and the line QR on 0.

Count along the scale that starts at 0 on QR up to 65 and make a dot P. Join Q to P.

Answer: ∠PQR = 65°

Turns and the clock face

TurnDegreesRight angles
14-turn90°1
12-turn180°2
34-turn270°3
whole turn360°4

Each hour space on a clock is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. At 2 o’clock the hands are 2 × 30° = 60° apart.

Adding and subtracting angles

Find the whole angle

∠PQR = 35° and ∠RQS = 60°. Find ∠PQS.

35° + 60° = 95°.

Answer: ∠PQS = 95°

Find a part

∠PQS = 95° and ∠PQR = 35°. Find ∠RQS.

95° − 35° = 60°. Check: 35° + 60° = 95°.

Answer: ∠RQS = 60°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading the wrong scale (130° for a 50° angle)Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm, then check your estimate
Writing ∠BAC for the angle at BPut the vertex in the middle: ∠ABC
Thinking longer arms make a bigger angleThe size of an angle is the amount of turn, not the length of the arms
Putting the protractor centre at the end of an armPut the centre exactly on the vertex

faq.q: What do P4 students learn about angles?
faq.a: They name angles as ∠ABC or ∠a, tell acute, right and obtuse angles apart, measure and draw angles with a protractor, and link quarter, half and whole turns to 90°, 180° and 360°.

faq.q: How do you name an angle like ∠ABC?
faq.a: Use three letters with the vertex in the middle: ∠ABC is the angle at B between the arms BA and BC. ∠CBA is the same angle.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when using a protractor?
faq.a: Reading the wrong scale, for example 130° instead of 50°. Read the scale that starts at 0 on one arm, and check that an acute angle gets a reading below 90°.

faq.q: Is this topic in the MOE syllabus for Primary 4?
faq.a: Yes. Measuring and drawing angles in degrees and naming them with ∠ABC and ∠a are part of Geometry in the MOE 2021 Primary 4 syllabus. Angle facts such as angles on a straight line come in P5.

items.q: Name the marked angle.
items.e: Follow the arc. Its arms go to A and C, and the vertex is B. So the angle is ∠ABC. With three arms at B, a name like ∠B alone would not say which angle you mean.

items.q: In triangle XYZ, which angle is ∠XYZ?
items.e: In ∠XYZ the middle letter is Y, so the vertex is Y. The angle at Y is marked ∠b.

items.q: Name the marked angle.
items.e: Follow the arc. Its arms go to S and R, and the vertex is Q. So the angle is ∠SQR. With three arms at Q, a name like ∠Q alone would not say which angle you mean.

items.q: Which angle has its vertex at M?
items.e: The vertex is the middle letter. Only ∠LMN has M in the middle.
The vertex is Q, where the two arms meet. Put the vertex letter in the middle: ∠PQR (∠RQP is also correct). An angle name needs three letters.

items.q: Which two names are for the same angle?
items.e: Both names have Y in the middle, so both have the vertex at Y and the arms YX and YZ. You may read the angle from either arm.

items.q: Which is another name for ∠y?
items.e: ∠y is between the arms QR and QS. The vertex Q goes in the middle: ∠RQS. ∠PQR is ∠x, and ∠PQS is ∠x and ∠y together.

items.q: Name the marked angle.
items.e: Follow the arc. Its arms go to E and G, and the vertex is F. So the angle is ∠EFG. With three arms at F, a name like ∠F alone would not say which angle you mean.

items.q: In ∠PQR, which point is the vertex?
items.e: The middle letter of an angle name is always the vertex. In ∠PQR it is Q.
Follow the arc. Its arms go to K and N, and the vertex is L. So the angle is ∠KLN. With three arms at L, a name like ∠L alone would not say which angle you mean.

items.q: What are the two arms of ∠DEF?
items.e: The vertex is E, the middle letter. Both arms start at E: one goes to D and one goes to F.

items.q: Which angle is a right angle?
items.e: The small square shows a right angle. It sits between the arms BA and BC, so ∠ABC = 90°. ∠ABD is bigger than a right angle and ∠CBD is smaller.

items.q: ∠PQS is made up of ∠PQR and ∠RQS. Which of the three angles is the largest?
items.e: ∠PQS is the whole angle. ∠PQR and ∠RQS are its two parts, so each part is smaller than ∠PQS.

items.q: Name the marked angle.
items.e: The vertex is Y, where the two arms meet. Put the vertex letter in the middle: ∠XYZ (∠ZYX is also correct). An angle name needs three letters.

items.q: Name the marked angle.
items.e: The vertex is B, where the two arms meet. Put the vertex letter in the middle: ∠ABC (∠CBA is also correct). An angle name needs three letters.

items.q: ∠XOV is made up of which angles?
items.e: ∠XOV goes from arm OX all the way to arm OV. It is ∠m (∠XOW) and ∠n (∠WOV) put together.

items.q: Name the marked angle in the triangle.
items.e: The marked angle is at E. Its arms are ED and EF, so its name is ∠DEF, with E in the middle.

items.q: Which angle is ∠a?
items.e: ∠a is between the arms BA and BC, so ∠a = ∠ABC. ∠CBD is ∠b, and ∠ABD is the whole angle, ∠a and ∠b together.

items.q: The vertex of an angle is B and its arms go to A and C. Kavya names it ∠BAC. What is wrong?
c: B must be the middle letter
The letters must be in ABC order
items.e: ∠BAC has A in the middle, so it means the angle at A. The angle at B is ∠ABC (or ∠CBA).

items.q: Name the marked angle in the triangle.
items.e: The marked angle is at R. Its arms are RP and RQ, so its name is ∠PRQ, with R in the middle.

sets.title: Acute, right or obtuse? Estimate angles

items.e: The angle is bigger than a right angle (90°) but smaller than a straight line (180°), so it is obtuse. About 120° fits. (It is 118°.) 60° is the number on the other scale of a protractor.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is smaller than a right angle (90°), so it is acute. About 45° fits. (It is 43°.) 135° is the number on the other scale of a protractor.
The angle is bigger than a right angle (90°) but smaller than a straight line (180°), so it is obtuse. About 170° fits. (It is 172°.) 10° is the number on the other scale of a protractor.

items.q: Which angle is 90°?
items.e: The small square in B shows a right angle, 90°. A and D are obtuse and C is acute.
The size of an angle is the amount of turn, not the length of the arms. A opens the widest (about 150°), so it is the largest, even though its arms are the shortest.

items.q: Which of these is an obtuse angle?
items.e: An obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°. Only 135° is. 90° is a right angle; 45° and 85° are acute.
The angle is bigger than a right angle (90°) but smaller than a straight line (180°), so it is obtuse. About 150° fits. (It is 147°.) 30° is the number on the other scale of a protractor.

items.q: Is the marked angle acute, right or obtuse?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 55°. Turning an angle does not change its size.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is smaller than a right angle (90°), so it is acute. About 60° fits. (It is 62°.) 120° is the number on the other scale of a protractor.
The two arms make a straight line: 180°, half a turn.

items.q: Is the marked angle acute, right or obtuse?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 35°.

items.q: Which angle is obtuse?
items.e: Obtuse means more than a right angle (90°) and less than 180°. Only C opens wider than a right angle. B is close to a right angle, but a little smaller, so it is acute.

items.q: An angle is a little smaller than a right angle. Which could it be?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. A little smaller than 90° is about 80°. 100° is a little bigger, and 8° is very small.

items.q: Is the marked angle acute, right or obtuse?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 70°. Turning an angle does not change its size.

items.q: Is the marked angle acute, right or obtuse?
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a quarter turn. The small square shows it. Turning an angle does not change its size.

items.q: Which angle is bigger?
items.e: Look at how wide the arms open, not how long they are. ∠q opens wider (70°) than ∠p (40°). Longer arms do not make a bigger angle.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 100°. Turning an angle does not change its size.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is smaller than a right angle (90°), so it is acute. About 30° fits. (It is 28°.) 150° is the number on the other scale of a protractor.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 125°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 160°.

sets.title: Read a protractor: inner and outer scales

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 30. (The inner scale says 150 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 30° makes sense.

items.q: One arm of an angle is on 0 of the outer scale. Which scale should you read?
c: the scale with the bigger number
the scale with the smaller number
items.e: Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm. Here that is the outer scale.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 40 and the other is at 150. The angle is the difference: 150° − 40° = 110°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 145. The marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 140 and 150 is 145. (The inner scale says 35 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 145° makes sense.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 20 and the other is at 95. The angle is the difference: 95° − 20° = 75°.

items.q: Wei Ming measures an angle that is clearly smaller than a right angle. The other arm crosses the protractor at 35 and 145. What is the angle?
items.e: An angle smaller than a right angle is less than 90°, so it is 35°. 145 is on the other scale.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 55. The marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 50 and 60 is 55. (The inner scale says 125 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 55° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 120. (The inner scale says 60 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 120° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 110. The outer scale says 70 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 110° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 70. (The inner scale says 110 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 70° makes sense.

items.q: Where do you put the centre of the protractor when you measure ∠ABC?
c: in the middle of the line AC
items.e: The centre goes on the vertex, where the two arms meet. In ∠ABC the vertex is the middle letter, B. Then line up one arm with 0.

items.q: On the inner scale, one arm of an angle is at 20 and the other arm is at 75. What is the angle?
items.e: Neither arm is on 0, so find the difference: 75° − 20° = 55°. (95° comes from adding, and 105° is what the outer scale shows for 75.)

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 155. The marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 150 and 160 is 155. The outer scale says 25 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 155° makes sense.

items.q: Raju measures an angle that is clearly obtuse and writes 70°. What is the angle?
items.e: An obtuse angle is more than 90°, so 70° cannot be right. Raju read the wrong scale. The other scale shows 180 − 70 = 110 at the same place, so the angle is 110°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 135. The marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 130 and 140 is 135. The outer scale says 45 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 135° makes sense.

items.q: Ali wants to draw an angle of 65°. He puts his line on 0 of the inner scale. Where should he make a dot?
items.e: Use the scale that starts at 0 on your line: the inner scale. Count up to 65 (the mark between 60 and 70), make a dot, then join it to the vertex. Using 65 on the outer scale would give 115°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 80. The outer scale says 100 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 80° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 65. The marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 60 and 70 is 65. The outer scale says 115 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 65° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 100. (The inner scale says 80 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 100° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 40. The outer scale says 140 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 40° makes sense.

sets.title: Turns and angles on a clock face

items.q: The minute hand turns through 180°. How many minutes have passed?
items.e: 180° is a half turn. The minute hand makes a half turn in half an hour: 30 minutes.

items.q: What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 3 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 numbers on a clock split a whole turn (360°) into 12 equal spaces: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° each. The hands are 3 spaces apart: 3 × 30° = 90°. At 3 o’clock the hands make a right angle (a quarter turn).

items.q: How many degrees are in a half turn?
items.e: A half turn is half of 360°: 360° ÷ 2 = 180°. The arms make a straight line.

items.q: What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 5 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 numbers on a clock split a whole turn (360°) into 12 equal spaces: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° each. The hands are 5 spaces apart: 5 × 30° = 150°.

items.q: How many degrees are in a quarter turn?
items.e: A whole turn is 360°. A quarter of it is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°, a right angle.

items.q: How many right angles make a half turn?
items.e: A half turn is 180°, and 2 × 90° = 180°.

items.q: How many degrees are in a 34-turn?
items.e: A quarter turn is 90°, so three quarter turns are 3 × 90° = 270°. (75° is three quarters of 100, but a whole turn is 360°.)

items.q: What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 1 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 numbers on a clock split a whole turn (360°) into 12 equal spaces: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° each. The hands are 1 space apart: 1 × 30° = 30°.

items.q: Mei Ling faces north. She makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which way does she face now?
items.e: Clockwise from north, a quarter turn (90°) takes you to east. (Anticlockwise would be west.)

items.q: The minute hand turns for 30 minutes. How much of a turn is that?
items.e: The minute hand makes a whole turn in 60 minutes. 30 minutes is half of 60 minutes, so it is a half turn (180°).

items.q: What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 10 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 numbers on a clock split a whole turn (360°) into 12 equal spaces: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° each. The hands are 2 spaces apart: 2 × 30° = 60°. Count the short way, from 10 to 12: 2 spaces. (300° is the long way round.)

items.q: Kumar faces south at East Coast Park. He turns 180°. Which way does he face now?
items.e: 180° is a half turn. After a half turn you face the opposite way: south becomes north.

items.q: What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 6 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 numbers on a clock split a whole turn (360°) into 12 equal spaces: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° each. The hands are 6 spaces apart: 6 × 30° = 180°. At 6 o’clock the hands make a straight line: half a turn.

items.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 45 minutes?
items.e: 15 minutes is a quarter turn (90°). 45 minutes is 3 quarter turns: 3 × 90° = 270°.

items.q: How many right angles make a whole turn?
items.e: 4 × 90° = 360°, so 4 right angles make a whole turn. 2 right angles make a half turn.

items.q: The minute hand turns clockwise from 12 to 3. How many degrees does it turn?
items.e: From 12 to 3 is a quarter of the clock face: a quarter turn, 90°.

items.q: What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 2 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 numbers on a clock split a whole turn (360°) into 12 equal spaces: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° each. The hands are 2 spaces apart: 2 × 30° = 60°.

items.q: What is the smaller angle between the two hands at 4 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 numbers on a clock split a whole turn (360°) into 12 equal spaces: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° each. The hands are 4 spaces apart: 4 × 30° = 120°.

items.q: What fraction of a whole turn is 90°?
items.e: 90° × 4 = 360°, so 90° is 14 of a whole turn.

items.q: Siti faces east. She turns 90° anticlockwise. Which way does she face now?
items.e: Anticlockwise from east, a quarter turn takes you to north. (Clockwise would be south.)

sets.title: Angle problems: add and subtract marked angles

items.q: ∠DEG = 125°. Find the unknown angle ∠FEG.
items.e: The whole angle ∠DEG is 125°. Take away the part you know: 125° − 30° = 95°. Check: 30° + 95° = 125°.

items.q: Find ∠PQS.
items.e: ∠PQS is made up of ∠PQR and ∠RQS. Add them: 65° + 80° = 145°.

items.q: ∠PQS = 120°. Find the unknown angle ∠RQS.
items.e: The whole angle ∠PQS is 120°. Take away the part you know: 120° − 65° = 55°. Check: 65° + 55° = 120°.

items.q: Hui Min measures ∠ABC = 65° and ∠CBD = 40°. Together they make ∠ABD. Find ∠ABD.
items.e: ∠ABD is made up of ∠ABC and ∠CBD: 65° + 40° = 105°. (25° comes from subtracting.)

items.q: A robot at the Science Centre makes a quarter turn and then a half turn, both clockwise. How many degrees does it turn altogether?
items.e: A quarter turn is 90° and a half turn is 180°. 90° + 180° = 270°, a 34-turn.

items.q: ∠p and ∠q make 120° together. ∠p is twice as big as ∠q. Find ∠q.
items.e: ∠p is 2 units and ∠q is 1 unit, so 3 units = 120°. 1 unit = 120° ÷ 3 = 40°. ∠q = 40° (∠p = 80°). (60° comes from 120° ÷ 2.)

items.q: The minute hand of a clock turns from 12 to 2, and then from 2 to 5. How many degrees does it turn altogether?
items.e: Each hour space is 30°. From 12 to 2 is 2 × 30° = 60°, and from 2 to 5 is 3 × 30° = 90°. 60° + 90° = 150°.

items.q: Mdm Wong opens a paper fan to 150°. She first opened it to 50°. How many more degrees did she open it?
items.e: The whole is 150° and one part is 50°. The other part is 150° − 50° = 100°.

items.q: Farah cuts a round cake for Children’s Day into 4 equal pieces from the centre. What angle does each piece make at the centre?
items.e: The pieces go all the way round the centre: a whole turn, 360°. 360° ÷ 4 = 90°, a right angle. (45° comes from using 180°, and 360° is the whole turn before dividing.)

items.q: Find ∠ABD.
items.e: ∠ABD is made up of ∠ABC and ∠CBD. Add them: 35° + 50° = 85°.

items.q: The blades of Devi’s scissors are open at 25°. She opens them 15° more. What is the angle between the blades now?
items.e: Devi opens the blades more, so add: 25° + 15° = 40°.

items.q: ∠XYW = 135°. Find the unknown angle ∠ZYW.
items.e: The whole angle ∠XYW is 135°. Take away the part you know: 135° − 70° = 65°. Check: 70° + 65° = 135°.

items.q: ∠PQR is a right angle. Find ∠SQR.
items.e: A right angle is 90°. ∠SQR = 90° − 35° = 55°.

items.q: Two roads meet at an angle of 125°. A new footpath splits this angle into two parts. One part is 70°. Find the other part.
items.e: The whole is 125° and one part is 70°. The other part is 125° − 70° = 55°. (195° comes from adding instead of subtracting.)

items.q: A door is open at 40°. Mr Tan pushes it open another 75°. How wide is the door open now?
items.e: The model shows the two turns joined together. 40° + 75° = 115°.

items.q: ∠ABD = 110°. Find the unknown angle ∠CBD.
items.e: The whole angle ∠ABD is 110°. Take away the part you know: 110° − 45° = 65°. Check: 45° + 65° = 110°.

items.q: Find ∠KLN.
items.e: ∠KLN is made up of ∠KLM and ∠MLN. Add them: 40° + 80° = 120°.

items.q: ∠x and ∠y make a right angle together. ∠x is 20° more than ∠y. Find ∠y.
items.e: Take away the extra 20°: 90° − 20° = 70°. That is 2 equal units, so 1 unit = 70° ÷ 2 = 35°. ∠y = 35° (∠x = 55°). (45° comes from forgetting the extra 20°.)

items.q: Find ∠EFH.
items.e: ∠EFH is made up of ∠EFG and ∠GFH. Add them: 55° + 45° = 100°.

items.q: ∠ABC is a right angle. Find ∠DBC.
items.e: A right angle is 90°. ∠DBC = 90° − 60° = 30°.
